outcomes.question: We are preparing an annual return now. Must we check the particulars of auditors as well as directors?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ACRA annual return officer particulars and CEO role confirmation** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** From 20 October 2026, an annual-return filer must confirm that current particulars already provided to ACRA are accurate for directors, chief executive officers (CEOs), secretaries, auditors and relevant members. These particulars include names, identification details, nationality, contact address, appointment dates, registered office address and shareholding details where applicable. The form separately asks whether any individual performs the CEO role. A company limited by guarantee must confirm its latest-reported total member count. Applies to annual returns filed from the expressly stated commencement date. Check ACRA-recorded particulars and update inaccurate particulars in Bizfile before filing. The CEO question concerns individuals performing the role; the ACRA notice does not limit it to a title or appointed position. Companies limited by guarantee have an additional total-number-of-members confirmation. The notice does not say the CEO question or officer-particulars confirmation changes the underlying duty to appoint or register officers. A case-specific conclusion requires: For a particular filing: filing date, company type, existing ACRA particulars, whether individuals perform the CEO role, and whether the company is limited by guarantee. General change explanation only; does not verify what particulars are currently recorded for an entity. Do not apply this change to filings submitted before 20 October 2026 without contemporaneous evidence. The notice gives examples of particulars and says “where applicable”; it is not a field-by-field eform schema. [ACRA | Commencement of Key Changes under the Corporate and Accounting Laws (Amendment) Act 2025 on 20 October 2026](https://www.acra.gov.sg/news-events/news-announcements/commencement-of-key-changes-under-the-corporate-and-accounting-laws--amendment--act-2025-on-20-october-2026/)

**Source:** ACRA | Commencement of Key Changes under the Corporate and Accounting Laws (Amendment) Act 2025 on 20 October 2026 (live external; from 20/10/2026)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ACRA annual return officer particulars and CEO role confirmation): The next phase of amendments under the Corporate and Accounting Laws (Amendment) Act 2025 will commence on 20 October 2026.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ACRA annual return officer particulars and CEO role confirmation): Companies filing annual returns will need to confirm that the latest particulars provided to ACRA are accurate for their directors, chief executive officers, secretaries, auditors and relevant members.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ACRA annual return officer particulars and CEO role confirmation): These include particulars such as names, identification details, nationality, contact address, appointment dates, registered office address and shareholding details, where applicable.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ACRA annual return officer particulars and CEO role confirmation): There will also be an additional question in the annual return eform for the filer to indicate if there are any individuals performing the role of Chief Executive Officer (CEO) in the company.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ACRA annual return officer particulars and CEO role confirmation): For companies limited by guarantee, filers will need to confirm that the total number of members last provided to ACRA through Bizfile is accurate.
- Official source: [ACRA | Commencement of Key Changes under the Corporate and Accounting Laws (Amendment) Act 2025 on 20 October 2026](https://www.acra.gov.sg/news-events/news-announcements/commencement-of-key-changes-under-the-corporate-and-accounting-laws--amendment--act-2025-on-20-october-2026/)

**Source:** ACRA | Deadline & requirements for annual returns (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ACRA annual return officer particulars and CEO role confirmation): All companies registered in Singapore must file an annual return with ACRA each year. This applies as long as your company is listed as “live” with us.
- Official source: [ACRA | Deadline & requirements for annual returns](https://www.acra.gov.sg/manage/companies/legal-requirements-common-offences/filing-annual-returns-companies/deadline-requirements/)

sources.documentTitle: ACRA | Commencement of Key Changes under the Corporate and Accounting Laws (Amendment) Act 2025 on 20 October 2026
sources.sourceText:
The next phase of amendments under the Corporate and Accounting Laws (Amendment) Act 2025 will commence on 20 October 2026.

Companies filing annual returns will need to confirm that the latest particulars provided to ACRA are accurate for their directors, chief executive officers, secretaries, auditors and relevant members.

These include particulars such as names, identification details, nationality, contact address, appointment dates, registered office address and shareholding details, where applicable.

There will also be an additional question in the annual return eform for the filer to indicate if there are any individuals performing the role of Chief Executive Officer (CEO) in the company.

For companies limited by guarantee, filers will need to confirm that the total number of members last provided to ACRA through Bizfile is accurate.

sources.documentTitle: ACRA | Deadline & requirements for annual returns
sources.sourceText:
An annual return is an online form you have to file with ACRA.

It contains key details about your company, such as:

Company name and registration number

Company type, business activities, and registered office address

Details of directors, the company secretary, and members

Share information and financial statements (if required)

This information helps stakeholders (like investors and partners) to make informed decisions.

Annual filing requirements

Company officers must file annual returns on time to avoid enforcement action.

Company requirements

Filing requirement

Details

Annual return filing with ACRA

All companies registered in Singapore must file an annual return with ACRA each year. This applies as long as your company is listed as “live” with us.

You must file an annual return even if your company is:

Inactive or dormant

Granted a tax waiver by the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS)

Filing your annual return keeps your company’s public information accurate. As a director, it is your legal duty to file on time.

Tax filing with IRAS

After filing your annual return, you must still file your taxes with IRAS. Check IRAS filing due dates and guides (opens in new tab).

Note: Dormant companies must also file tax returns unless IRAS has granted a waiver. Learn more about filing requirements for dormant companies (opens in new tab).

When to file your annual returns

Your deadline for filing the Annual Return is based on:

Your company's FYE

Your company type (listed or non-listed company)

Filing deadlines

Company type

Filing deadline

Listed companies

Within five months after FYE

Listed companies with:

A share capital

An overseas branch register

Within six months after FYE

Non-listed companies

Within seven months after FYE

Non-listed companies with:

A share capital

An overseas branch register

Within eight months after FYE

Note: You must file your annual returns on time to avoid penalties. You cannot change your FYE after the filing deadline has passed.

sources.sourceText:
The next phase of amendments under the Corporate and Accounting Laws (Amendment) Act 2025 will commence on 20 October 2026.

Companies filing annual returns will need to confirm that the latest particulars provided to ACRA are accurate for their directors, chief executive officers, secretaries, auditors and relevant members.

These include particulars such as names, identification details, nationality, contact address, appointment dates, registered office address and shareholding details, where applicable.

There will also be an additional question in the annual return eform for the filer to indicate if there are any individuals performing the role of Chief Executive Officer (CEO) in the company.

For companies limited by guarantee, filers will need to confirm that the total number of members last provided to ACRA through Bizfile is accurate.

outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ACRA annual return officer particulars and CEO role confirmation** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** From 20 October 2026, an annual-return filer must confirm that current particulars already provided to ACRA are accurate for directors, chief executive officers (CEOs), secretaries, auditors and relevant members. These particulars include names, identification details, nationality, contact address, appointment dates, registered office address and shareholding details where applicable. The form separately asks whether any individual performs the CEO role. A company limited by guarantee must confirm its latest-reported total member count. Applies to annual returns filed from the expressly stated commencement date. Check ACRA-recorded particulars and update inaccurate particulars in Bizfile before filing. The CEO question concerns individuals performing the role; the ACRA notice does not limit it to a title or appointed position. Companies limited by guarantee have an additional total-number-of-members confirmation. The notice does not say the CEO question or officer-particulars confirmation changes the underlying duty to appoint or register officers. A case-specific conclusion requires: For a particular filing: filing date, company type, existing ACRA particulars, whether individuals perform the CEO role, and whether the company is limited by guarantee. General change explanation only; does not verify what particulars are currently recorded for an entity. Do not apply this change to filings submitted before 20 October 2026 without contemporaneous evidence. The notice gives examples of particulars and says “where applicable”; it is not a field-by-field eform schema. The stated commencement does not make this new change applicable to the filing date supplied before 20 October 2026. This notice does not establish the complete requirements that governed that earlier filing. outcomes.question: Is a solvent exempt private company automatically required to upload Full XBRL financial statements?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ACRA XBRL financial statement filing requirements and exemptions** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** The ACRA guidance lists simplified XBRL plus an authorised PDF for smaller and non-publicly accountable companies; XBRL FSH (Banks) or XBRL FSH (Insurance) plus an authorised PDF for the regulated bank, finance and insurance group; PDF only for companies limited by guarantee or companies approved to use other standards; and Full XBRL for all other Singapore-incorporated companies required to file financial statements. “Smaller” requires both current-year revenue and assets not exceeding S$500,000. “Non-publicly accountable” also excludes listed and specified regulated entity types. The dormant-relevant-company and solvent-EPC financial-statement exceptions have separate qualification conditions. ACRA labels technical resources as applying from 19 October 2026 onwards and identifies ACRA Taxonomy 2026 resources. A company must first determine whether it is required to file financial statements; dormant relevant companies and solvent EPCs may qualify for separate financial-statement exceptions. Small-company revenue and asset thresholds must both be met; group consolidation and currency translation details apply under the ACRA definitions page. The Full/Simplified/FSH/PDF template depends on the company’s exact status and regulatory category. Dormant relevant companies need not prepare/file only if all Companies Act section 201A requirements are met, including the assets, dormancy and listing/subsidiary conditions. A solvent EPC meeting an EPC definition may elect not to file financial statements but may file voluntarily; its annual-return solvency declaration still applies. Foreign companies with Singapore branches and some individually approved cases are addressed elsewhere on the ACRA filing guidance and are not classified by this local-company rule summary. A case-specific conclusion requires: Local/foreign incorporation, company form and whether it is a company limited by guarantee. Required-to-file/exempt status, dormancy history, listed/subsidiary status and group assets. Current-year revenue and assets, consolidation and currency facts. Public-accountability or MAS regulatory status. EPC status and solvency, where relevant. Does not determine an individual company’s template without classification facts. The complete definitions and section 201A eligibility must be checked against ACRA’s linked guidance and law. Do not apply the current page or 19 October 2026 XBRL boundary to a historical filing unless the relevant year-specific official source supports it. [ACRA | Financial statements: Filing requirements and exemptions](https://www.acra.gov.sg/manage/companies/legal-requirements-common-offences/filing-financial-statements-in-xbrl-format/requirements-exemptions/)

**Source:** ACRA | Financial statements: Filing requirements and exemptions (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ACRA XBRL financial statement filing requirements and exemptions): Smaller and non-publicly accountable companies, including insolvent EPCs that cannot pay their debts as and when they are due:
Simplified XBRL financial statements; and a PDF copy of your financial statements authorised by directors.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ACRA XBRL financial statement filing requirements and exemptions): Banks, finance and insurance companies:
XBRL FSH (Banks) or XBRL FSH (Insurance) financial statements; and a PDF copy of your financial statements authorised by directors.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ACRA XBRL financial statement filing requirements and exemptions): Companies limited by guarantee; or companies using other accounting standards upon approval by ACRA:
PDF copy of your financial statements authorised by directors.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ACRA XBRL financial statement filing requirements and exemptions): All other Singapore-incorporated companies, including insolvent EPCs that are not small and non-publicly accountable and are required to file financial statements:
Full XBRL financial statements.

- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ACRA XBRL financial statement filing requirements and exemptions): You do not need to prepare and file financial statements if your company meets all of the requirements under section 201A of the Companies Act.

- Official source: [ACRA | Financial statements: Filing requirements and exemptions](https://www.acra.gov.sg/manage/companies/legal-requirements-common-offences/filing-financial-statements-in-xbrl-format/requirements-exemptions/)

**Source:** Audit Exemptions: Small Company Concept | Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA) (offline fixture title) (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ACRA XBRL financial statement filing requirements and exemptions): Learn when your private company qualifies for audit exemption under the small company concept. This exemption applies to financial years beginning on or after 1 July 2015.
Last updated on 3 February 2026
On this page
Who qualifies for audit exemption
Maintaining your exemption status
Frequently asked questions (FAQs)
Who qualifies for audit exemption
To qualify for audit exemption as a small company, you need to meet both of these criteria:
Your company is a private company in the financial year; and
Your company meets at least two of these quantitative criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years:
Total annual revenue of $10 million or less, based on your financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting standards
Total assets of $10 million or less, based on your financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting standards
50 employees or fewer, based on the number of full-time employees at the end of your financial year
Detailed exemption criteria
If your company is newly incorporated (less than two years old)
You qualify for audit exemption if you meet the criteria in the current financial year.
Example:
First financial year: Check if you are a private company and meet two out of three quantitative criteria that year.
Second financial year: If you did not qualify in the first year, check again using the same requirements for the second year.
If your company is part of a group
You need to meet both of these conditions to qualify for audit exemption:
Your Singapore company or subsidiary qualifies as a small company; and
Your entire group (including foreign entities) meets at least two of these quantitative criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years:
Total annual revenue of $10 million or less, based on your holding company's consolidated financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting standards
Total assets of $10 million or less, based on your holding company's consolidated financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting standards
50 employees or fewer, based on the number of full-time employees at the end of your financial year
Note: The audit exemption applies to financial years beginning on or after 1 July 2015.
Maintaining your exemption status
Once your company qualifies as a small company, you remain qualified in subsequent financial years unless:
You cease to be a private company at any time during a financial year; or
You do not meet at least two out of three criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years
Once your group qualifies as a small group, it remains qualified for subsequent financial years. This applies until it does not meet at least two out of three criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years.
Frequently asked questions (FAQs)
Can companies with corporate shareholders get audit exemption?
Yes, you can qualify for audit exemption even if you have corporate shareholders.
Unlike the previous criteria, you do not need to be an exempt private company to qualify for audit exemption.
Does the small company criteria affect financial statement filing?
No, it does not change your financial statement filing requirements.
- Official source: [Audit Exemptions: Small Company Concept | Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA) (offline fixture title)](https://www.acra.gov.sg/manage/companies/legal-requirements-common-offences/preparing-financial-statements/audit-exemptions/)

verifiedClaims.text:
Learn when your private company qualifies for audit exemption under the small company concept. This exemption applies to financial years beginning on or after 1 July 2015.
Last updated on 3 February 2026
On this page
Who qualifies for audit exemption
Maintaining your exemption status
Frequently asked questions (FAQs)
Who qualifies for audit exemption
To qualify for audit exemption as a small company, you need to meet both of these criteria:
Your company is a private company in the financial year; and
Your company meets at least two of these quantitative criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years:
Total annual revenue of $10 million or less, based on your financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting standards
Total assets of $10 million or less, based on your financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting standards
50 employees or fewer, based on the number of full-time employees at the end of your financial year
Detailed exemption criteria
If your company is newly incorporated (less than two years old)
You qualify for audit exemption if you meet the criteria in the current financial year.
Example:
First financial year: Check if you are a private company and meet two out of three quantitative criteria that year.
Second financial year: If you did not qualify in the first year, check again using the same requirements for the second year.
If your company is part of a group
You need to meet both of these conditions to qualify for audit exemption:
Your Singapore company or subsidiary qualifies as a small company; and
Your entire group (including foreign entities) meets at least two of these quantitative criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years:
Total annual revenue of $10 million or less, based on your holding company's consolidated financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting standards
Total assets of $10 million or less, based on your holding company's consolidated financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting standards
50 employees or fewer, based on the number of full-time employees at the end of your financial year
Note: The audit exemption applies to financial years beginning on or after 1 July 2015.
Maintaining your exemption status
Once your company qualifies as a small company, you remain qualified in subsequent financial years unless:
You cease to be a private company at any time during a financial year; or
You do not meet at least two out of three criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years
Once your group qualifies as a small group, it remains qualified for subsequent financial years. This applies until it does not meet at least two out of three criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years.
Frequently asked questions (FAQs)
Can companies with corporate shareholders get audit exemption?
Yes, you can qualify for audit exemption even if you have corporate shareholders.
Unlike the previous criteria, you do not need to be an exempt private company to qualify for audit exemption.
Does the small company criteria affect financial statement filing?
No, it does not change your financial statement filing requirements.

sources.sourceText:
Smaller and non-publicly accountable companies, including insolvent EPCs that cannot pay their debts as and when they are due:
Simplified XBRL financial statements; and a PDF copy of your financial statements authorised by directors.

Banks, finance and insurance companies:
XBRL FSH (Banks) or XBRL FSH (Insurance) financial statements; and a PDF copy of your financial statements authorised by directors.

Companies limited by guarantee; or companies using other accounting standards upon approval by ACRA:
PDF copy of your financial statements authorised by directors.

All other Singapore-incorporated companies, including insolvent EPCs that are not small and non-publicly accountable and are required to file financial statements:
Full XBRL financial statements.

XBRL filing requirements (from 19 October 2026 onwards).

All Singapore-incorporated companies must:

Prepare financial statements, except dormant relevant companies.

You do not need to prepare and file financial statements if your company meets all of the requirements under section 201A of the Companies Act.

Revenue for the current financial year does not exceed $500,000.

Total assets for the current financial year do not exceed $500,000.

Private company: You have fewer than 20 members and no corporation holds beneficial interest in your shares (directly or indirectly).

Solvent exempt private company (EPC)

Your company is non-publicly accountable if it is:

Your Singapore company or subsidiary qualifies as a small company; and
Your entire group (including foreign entities) meets at least two of these quantitative criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years:
Total annual revenue of $10 million or less, based on your holding company's consolidated financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting standards
Total assets of $10 million or less, based on your holding company's consolidated financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting standards
50 employees or fewer, based on the number of full-time employees at the end of your financial year
Note: The audit exemption applies to financial years beginning on or after 1 July 2015.
Maintaining your exemption status
Once your company qualifies as a small company, you remain qualified in subsequent financial years unless:
You cease to be a private company at any time during a financial year; or
You do not meet at least two out of three criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years
Once your group qualifies as a small group, it remains qualified for subsequent financial years. This applies until it does not meet at least two out of three criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years.
Frequently asked questions (FAQs)
Can companies with corporate shareholders get audit exemption?
Yes, you can qualify for audit exemption even if you have corporate shareholders.
Unlike the previous criteria, you do not need to be an exempt private company to qualify for audit exemption.
Does the small company criteria affect financial statement filing?
No, it does not change your financial statement filing requirements.

outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for the issues identified below; other issues remain incomplete.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** See the evidence gaps and coverage limitations below.

#### IRAS — GST

**Status:** Evidence verified

**GST input tax on staff medical expenses** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS states that staff medical input tax is generally disallowed under regulation 26 of the GST (General) Regulations. Subject to the ordinary input-tax conditions, the stated exceptions are expenses obligatory under WICA or a qualifying Industrial Relations Act collective agreement; or, for expenses incurred on or after 1 October 2021, treatment connected with a work-related health risk or requirement and required under relevant Singapore written law. For the advisory limb, IRAS specifies treatment related to COVID-19 and required under a written advisory of the Government or a Singapore public authority. IRAS specifically says Primary Care Plan expenses do not meet the described work-related exception. A claim needs the expense date, legal/collective-agreement basis, work-related risk and mandate evidence, GST registration and invoice facts. [IRAS | Conditions for Claiming Input Tax](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/goods-services-tax-(gst)/claiming-gst-(input-tax)/conditions-for-claiming-input-tax)

**Source:** IRAS | Conditions for Claiming Input Tax (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports GST input tax on staff medical expenses): Input tax claims are disallowed under Regulation 26 of the GST (General) Regulations.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports GST input tax on staff medical expenses): However, subject to the conditions for input tax claim, these claims are allowed if: • the medical expenses (e.g. pre-employment and annual health screening expenses) are obligatory under the Work Injury Compensation Act (WICA) or under any collective agreement under the Industrial Relations Act (IRA); or • the medical treatment in respect of expenses incurred on or after 1 Oct 2021 is provided in connection with any health risk or requirement due to the work nature or environment and mandated by written law or advisory.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports GST input tax on staff medical expenses): the medical treatment in respect of expenses incurred on or after 1 Oct 2021 is provided in connection with any health risk or requirement arising on account of the nature of the work required of your staff or his work environment; and ◦ the medical expenses are incurred pursuant to any written law of Singapore concerning the medical treatment or the provision of a medical facility or medical practitioner; or ◦ the medical treatment is related to COVID-19 and the staff undergoes such medical treatment pursuant to any written advisory (including industry circular) issued by, or posted on the website of, the Government or a public authority of Singapore.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports GST input tax on staff medical expenses): No, GST incurred on PCP will not be claimable. Based on the nature of the medical expenses covered under the PCP, the medical treatment is not provided in connection with any health risk or requirement arising on account of the nature of the work required of your staff or his work environment (e.g. employees exposed to radiation in the course of their work are required to undergo prescribed medical examinations by an approved medical practitioner). As such, it does not fall under any of the exceptions above and thus GST incurred on PCP will not be claimable.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports GST input tax on staff medical expenses): Can I claim the GST charged on medical examinations incurred for the purpose of renewing my employees' work permits? No, the input tax on such examinations is blocked as medical expenses under Regulation 26 of the GST (General) Regulations.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports GST input tax on staff medical expenses): Input tax claims are disallowed under Regulation 26 of the GST (General) Regulations. However, subject to the conditions for input tax claim, these claims are allowed if: • the medical expenses (e.g. pre-employment and annual health screening expenses) are obligatory under the Work Injury Compensation Act (WICA) or under any collective agreement under the Industrial Relations Act (IRA); or • the medical treatment in respect of expenses incurred on or after 1 Oct 2021 is provided in connection with any health risk or requirement due to the work nature or environment and mandated by written law or advisory.
- Official source: [IRAS | Conditions for Claiming Input Tax](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/goods-services-tax-(gst)/claiming-gst-(input-tax)/conditions-for-claiming-input-tax)

**Source:** GST (General) Regulations (local static)
- **Reviewed local summary** (supports GST input tax on staff medical expenses): Regulations 26 and 27 generally disallow input tax on specified expenses, subject to the scope limits and exceptions in the regulations and IRAS guidance. Business purpose alone does not make a blocked claim recoverable.

outcomes.question: Can a business recover GST on a chauffeured point-to-point private-hire ride instead of buying or hiring the motor car itself?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### IRAS — GST

**Status:** Evidence verified

**GST input tax on business motor cars** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS generally disallows input tax on a motor car’s purchase and running costs under regulation 27, unless the vehicle is outside the regulation 25(1) motor-car definition or a specific exception applies. Its examples include qualifying chauffeured pay-per-trip transport services from 1 April 2022; qualifying costs for cars used by a third party from 1 January 2023; and vehicles such as lorries, vans and motorcycles that are not motor cars. Costs for cars used physically or economically by you or your employees remain disallowed. For a connected person’s car, the claimant must recover the expense and the recovery must not be ancillary to a primary supply; partial recovery limits the claim to the recovered portion. If only half the expenses are recovered, the exception permits input tax only to the extent of that half, not the unrecovered half. All exceptions remain subject to the ordinary claim conditions and records. [IRAS | Conditions for Claiming Input Tax](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/goods-services-tax-(gst)/claiming-gst-(input-tax)/conditions-for-claiming-input-tax)

**Source:** IRAS | Conditions for Claiming Input Tax (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports GST input tax on business motor cars): Input tax claims on purchase and running expenses of motor cars are disallowed under Regulation 27 of the GST (General) Regulations unless the car is excluded from the definition of a 'motor car' in Regulation 25(1). In addition, input tax incurred for specific scenarios is also excluded from the scope of Regulation 27. The input tax incurred in such specific scenarios will be claimable, subject to the conditions for input tax claim.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports GST input tax on business motor cars): Yes, from 1 Apr 2022 onwards, you can claim input tax incurred on the purchase of services to transport passengers from point A to point B (pay-per-trip) in a chauffeured private hire car (e.g. airport transfer services), if the conditions for claiming input tax are met. Yes, you can claim input tax on the running expenses of your PHC incurred on or after 1 Jan 2023 in the course of providing the chauffeured ride services for a fee. However, the input tax incurred on private use of your PHC remains not claimable.

sources.sourceText:
Input tax claims on purchase and running expenses of motor cars are disallowed under Regulation 27 of the GST (General) Regulations unless the car is excluded from the definition of a 'motor car' in Regulation 25(1). In addition, input tax incurred for specific scenarios is also excluded from the scope of Regulation 27. The input tax incurred in such specific scenarios will be claimable, subject to the conditions for input tax claim.

Yes, from 1 Apr 2022 onwards, you can claim input tax incurred on the purchase of services to transport passengers from point A to point B (pay-per-trip) in a chauffeured private hire car (e.g. airport transfer services), if the conditions for claiming input tax are met. This includes ensuring that your purchases are supported by valid tax invoices or simplified tax invoices with GST charged to you. For example, for limousine services, you will need to keep an invoice from the GST-registered business showing that GST has been charged on the services.

Yes, from 1 Jan 2023, where you incur expenses on a motor car that is used by a third party, you will be allowed input tax claims on the cost and running expenses of the motor car incurred, if the conditions for claiming input tax are met

Input tax claims on motor car expenses for cars used by you or your employees are disallowed under Regulation 27 of the GST (General) Regulations. Use of the motor car includes both: • physical use (e.g. motor car driven by your company staff or chauffeur to transport your company directors or business associates); and • economic use (i.e., use of the car to generate income or make supplies e.g. a consultancy firm uses its motor car to transport its preferred clients for a fee).

No, from 1 Jan 2023, where you incur expenses on a motor car used by a person connected to you (e.g. your subsidiary), you cannot claim input tax on the cost and running expenses of the motor car, unless you satisfy both of the following conditions (in addition to the conditions for claiming input tax): 1. You recover the motor car expenses from the connected person. Where you recover only a portion of the motor car expenses incurred, you can only claim input tax to the extent of the portion recovered; and. 2. The recovery is not ancillary to any primary supply made by you to the connected person.

Yes, input tax claims are allowed on motor vehicles (e.g. lorry, van, motorcycle) that do not fall under the definition of a 'motor car'*, if the conditions for claiming input tax are met.

Input tax claims on purchase and running expenses of motor cars are disallowed under Regulation 27 of the GST (General) Regulations unless the car is excluded from the definition of a 'motor car' in Regulation 25(1). In addition, input tax incurred for specific scenarios is also excluded from the scope of Regulation 27. The input tax incurred in such specific scenarios will be claimable, subject to the conditions for input tax claim.

Yes, from 1 Apr 2022 onwards, you can claim input tax incurred on the purchase of services to transport passengers from point A to point B (pay-per-trip) in a chauffeured private hire car (e.g. airport transfer services), if the conditions for claiming input tax are met. This includes ensuring that your purchases are supported by valid tax invoices or simplified tax invoices with GST charged to you. For example, for limousine services, you will need to keep an invoice from the GST-registered business showing that GST has been charged on the services.

Yes, from 1 Jan 2023, where you incur expenses on a motor car that is used by a third party, you will be allowed input tax claims on the cost and running expenses of the motor car incurred, if the conditions for claiming input tax are met

Input tax claims on motor car expenses for cars used by you or your employees are disallowed under Regulation 27 of the GST (General) Regulations. Use of the motor car includes both: • physical use (e.g. motor car driven by your company staff or chauffeur to transport your company directors or business associates); and • economic use (i.e., use of the car to generate income or make supplies e.g. a consultancy firm uses its motor car to transport its preferred clients for a fee).

No, from 1 Jan 2023, where you incur expenses on a motor car used by a person connected to you (e.g. your subsidiary), you cannot claim input tax on the cost and running expenses of the motor car, unless you satisfy both of the following conditions (in addition to the conditions for claiming input tax): 1. You recover the motor car expenses from the connected person. Where you recover only a portion of the motor car expenses incurred, you can only claim input tax to the extent of the portion recovered; and. 2. The recovery is not ancillary to any primary supply made by you to the connected person.

Yes, input tax claims are allowed on motor vehicles (e.g. lorry, van, motorcycle) that do not fall under the definition of a 'motor car'*, if the conditions for claiming input tax are met.

- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS generally disallows input tax on a motor car’s purchase and running costs under regulation 27, unless the vehicle is outside the regulation 25(1) motor-car definition or a specific exception applies. Its examples include qualifying chauffeured pay-per-trip transport services from 1 April 2022; qualifying costs for cars used by a third party from 1 January 2023; and vehicles such as lorries, vans and motorcycles that are not motor cars. All exceptions remain subject to the ordinary claim conditions and records. In addition, input tax incurred for specific scenarios is also excluded from the scope of Regulation 27. The input tax incurred in such specific scenarios will be claimable, subject to the conditions for input tax claim.

Yes, from 1 Apr 2022 onwards, you can claim input tax incurred on the purchase of services to transport passengers from point A to point B (pay-per-trip) in a chauffeured private hire car (e.g. airport transfer services), if the conditions for claiming input tax are met. This includes ensuring that your purchases are supported by valid tax invoices or simplified tax invoices with GST charged to you. For example, for limousine services, you will need to keep an invoice from the GST-registered business showing that GST has been charged on the services.

No, from 1 Jan 2023, where you incur expenses on a motor car used by a person connected to you (e.g. your subsidiary), you cannot claim input tax on the cost and running expenses of the motor car, unless you satisfy both of the following conditions (in addition to the conditions for claiming input tax): 1. You recover the motor car expenses from the connected person. Where you recover only a portion of the motor car expenses incurred, you can only claim input tax to the extent of the portion recovered; and. 2. The recovery is not ancillary to any primary supply made by you to the connected person.

Yes, input tax claims are allowed on motor vehicles (e.g. lorry, van, motorcycle) that do not fall under the definition of a 'motor car'*, if the conditions for claiming input tax are met.

outcomes.question: If a treaty reduces withholding tax to zero, can we omit the WHT filing?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Withholding tax filing and payment deadline** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS requires WHT filing and payment by the 15th of the second month after its defined date of payment. For most payments, use the earliest of the contractual due date (or invoice date if there is no agreement, ignoring credit terms), credit to an account designated by the non-resident, and actual payment. Director fees have separate timing rules based on arrears/advance approval, entitlement, credit and actual payment. WHT still must be filed when a DTA or ARI makes the rate zero. GIRO is normally deducted on the 25th of the due month, or the next working day if that date is a weekend/public holiday. The exact deadline requires the payment type and all relevant dates. [IRAS | Withholding Tax (WHT) filing and payment due date](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/withholding-tax/withholding-tax-filing/withholding-tax-filing-and-payment-due-date)

**Source:** IRAS | Withholding Tax (WHT) filing and payment due date (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax filing and payment deadline): WHT must be filed even if the payment to a non-resident is exempted under the Avoidance of Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) or Approved Royalties Incentive (ARI).
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax filing and payment deadline): As a payer, you must file and pay WHT to IRAS by the 15th of the second month from the date of payment to the non-resident.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax filing and payment deadline): The date of payment is defined as the earliest of the following dates: For all payments except director's fees • When the payment is due and payable based on the agreement or contract, or the date of the invoice in the absence of any agreement or contract (credit terms should not be taken into consideration). • When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident • The date of actual payment
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax filing and payment deadline): For director's fees • When the payment is due and payable under the following scenarios: ◦ Director's fees approved in arrears For director's fees approved in arrears, the director has already rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned. However, the director's fees must be disclosed to and approved by members of the company before they can be paid to him. Hence, the earliest date on which the director is entitled to the director's fees, is the date the fees are voted and approved at the company's AGM. ◦ Director's fees approved in advance For director's fees approved in advance, the director may not have rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned when the fees are approved at the company's AGM. Hence, the earliest date on which the director can be entitled to the director's fees, is as and when he renders his services.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax filing and payment deadline): If you are on GIRO for WHT payment, the GIRO deduction date is on the 25th of the month the tax is due. If the GIRO deduction date falls on a weekend or public holiday, the deduction will be made on the next working day.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax filing and payment deadline): If you have made multiple payments to the same non-resident professional or non-resident public entertainer for the same engagement within a 60-day period, you can consolidate the various payments into 1 filing and declare the last payment date as the date of payment to the non-resident professional or public entertainer.
- Official source: [IRAS | Withholding Tax (WHT) filing and payment due date](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/withholding-tax/withholding-tax-filing/withholding-tax-filing-and-payment-due-date)

sources.sourceText:
WHT must be filed even if the payment to a non-resident is exempted under the Avoidance of Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) or Approved Royalties Incentive (ARI).

As a payer, you must file and pay WHT to IRAS by the 15th of the second month from the date of payment to the non-resident.

The date of payment is defined as the earliest of the following dates: For all payments except director's fees • When the payment is due and payable based on the agreement or contract, or the date of the invoice in the absence of any agreement or contract (credit terms should not be taken into consideration). • When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident • The date of actual payment

For director's fees • When the payment is due and payable under the following scenarios: ◦ Director's fees approved in arrears For director's fees approved in arrears, the director has already rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned. However, the director's fees must be disclosed to and approved by members of the company before they can be paid to him. Hence, the earliest date on which the director is entitled to the director's fees, is the date the fees are voted and approved at the company's AGM. ◦ Director's fees approved in advance For director's fees approved in advance, the director may not have rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned when the fees are approved at the company's AGM. Hence, the earliest date on which the director can be entitled to the director's fees, is as and when he renders his services.

If you are on GIRO for WHT payment, the GIRO deduction date is on the 25th of the month the tax is due. If the GIRO deduction date falls on a weekend or public holiday, the deduction will be made on the next working day.

If you have made multiple payments to the same non-resident professional or non-resident public entertainer for the same engagement within a 60-day period, you can consolidate the various payments into 1 filing and declare the last payment date as the date of payment to the non-resident professional or public entertainer.

Withholding Tax (WHT) Filing and Payment Due Date

Share:

•

•

•

•

•

•

Payers must file and pay the WHT to IRAS by the due date.

WHT must be filed even if the payment to a non-resident is exempted under the Avoidance of Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) or Approved Royalties Incentive (ARI).

On this page:

As a payer, you must file and pay WHT to IRAS by the 15th of the second month from the date of payment to the non-resident.

Learn more through our e-Learning video on the Filing and Payment of WHT.

If you are on GIRO for WHT payment, the GIRO deduction date is on the 25th of the month the tax is due. If the GIRO deduction date falls on a weekend or public holiday, the deduction will be made on the next working day.

Refer to your acknowledgement page for payment details after filing WHT.

Definition of date of payment

The date of payment is defined as the earliest of the following dates:

For all payments except director’s fees

• When the payment is due and payable based on the agreement or contract, or the date of the invoice in the absence of any agreement or contract (credit terms should not be taken into consideration).

• When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident

• The date of actual payment

For director’s fees

• When the payment is due and payable under the following scenarios:

◦ Director's fees approved in arrears

For director's fees approved in arrears, the director has already rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned. However, the director's fees must be disclosed to and approved by members of the company before they can be paid to him. Hence, the earliest date on which the director is entitled to the director's fees, is the date the fees are voted and approved at the company's AGM.

◦ Director's fees approved in advance

For director's fees approved in advance, the director may not have rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned when the fees are approved at the company's AGM. Hence, the earliest date on which the director can be entitled to the director's fees, is as and when he renders his services.

•

• When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident

• The date of actual payment

Scenarios | Date of payment to the non-resident  

Filing and payment due date

Technical assistance fees
A non-resident company issued an invoice dated 26 Mar 2025 to a payer for technical assistance fees in respect of services rendered. The invoice stated that the amount must be paid within 30 days.
The payer received the invoice on 30 Apr 2025 and paid the non-resident on 19 May 2025.  | 26 Mar 2025
(based on invoice date)  | 15 May 2025

For GIRO payer, deduction takes place on 26 May 2025.

Royalty payment
The agreement stated that royalties at 5% of sales shall accrue to the non-resident at the end of each quarter.
In this instance, the royalty period from Apr to Jun 2025 was accrued on 30 Jun 2025 (end of quarter), and the royalty payment was made to the non-resident on 15 Jul 2025. | 30 Jun 2025
(based on date of accrual)  | 15 Aug 2025

For GIRO payer, deduction takes place on 25 Aug 2025.

Director’s fee
The director’s fee of $50,000 for the period from 01 Jan 2024 to 31 Dec 2024, was voted and approved in the company's Annual General Meeting (AGM) on 2 Jul 2025.
However, the fee was only paid to the director on 29 Sep 2025.  | 2 Jul 2025
(based on AGM date)  | 15 Sep 2025

For GIRO payer, deduction takes place on 25 Sep 2025.

Multiple payments for a single engagement (non-resident professional or public entertainer)

If you have made multiple payments to the same non-resident professional or non-resident public entertainer for the same engagement within a 60-day period, you can consolidate the various payments into 1 filing and declare the last payment date as the date of payment to the non-resident professional or public entertainer.

Late payment penalty

Penalties will be imposed if the WHT is paid to IRAS after the payment due date or if the GIRO deduction is unsuccessful.

FAQs

Can I consolidate and file my WHT submission?

Yes, you can consolidate and file WHT twice a year, on 15 June and 15 December of each year if you are claiming tax exemption (i.e. tax rate is 0%) under the DTA and ARI.

For example:

Your WHT exempted (i.e. tax rate is 0%) payment to a non-resident is due every 15 of the month. Instead of filing for WHT monthly, you can consolidate and file 6 records on 15 June and the remaining 6 records on 15 December.

sources.sourceText:
WHT must be filed even if the payment to a non-resident is exempted under the Avoidance of Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) or Approved Royalties Incentive (ARI).

As a payer, you must file and pay WHT to IRAS by the 15th of the second month from the date of payment to the non-resident.

The date of payment is defined as the earliest of the following dates: For all payments except director's fees • When the payment is due and payable based on the agreement or contract, or the date of the invoice in the absence of any agreement or contract (credit terms should not be taken into consideration). • When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident • The date of actual payment

For director's fees • When the payment is due and payable under the following scenarios: ◦ Director's fees approved in arrears For director's fees approved in arrears, the director has already rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned. However, the director's fees must be disclosed to and approved by members of the company before they can be paid to him. Hence, the earliest date on which the director is entitled to the director's fees, is the date the fees are voted and approved at the company's AGM. ◦ Director's fees approved in advance For director's fees approved in advance, the director may not have rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned when the fees are approved at the company's AGM. Hence, the earliest date on which the director can be entitled to the director's fees, is as and when he renders his services.

If you are on GIRO for WHT payment, the GIRO deduction date is on the 25th of the month the tax is due. If the GIRO deduction date falls on a weekend or public holiday, the deduction will be made on the next working day.

If you have made multiple payments to the same non-resident professional or non-resident public entertainer for the same engagement within a 60-day period, you can consolidate the various payments into 1 filing and declare the last payment date as the date of payment to the non-resident professional or public entertainer.

Withholding Tax (WHT) Filing and Payment Due Date

Share:

•

•

•

•

•

•

Payers must file and pay the WHT to IRAS by the due date.

WHT must be filed even if the payment to a non-resident is exempted under the Avoidance of Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) or Approved Royalties Incentive (ARI).

On this page:

As a payer, you must file and pay WHT to IRAS by the 15th of the second month from the date of payment to the non-resident.

Learn more through our e-Learning video on the Filing and Payment of WHT.

If you are on GIRO for WHT payment, the GIRO deduction date is on the 25th of the month the tax is due. If the GIRO deduction date falls on a weekend or public holiday, the deduction will be made on the next working day.

Refer to your acknowledgement page for payment details after filing WHT.

Definition of date of payment

The date of payment is defined as the earliest of the following dates:

For all payments except director’s fees

• When the payment is due and payable based on the agreement or contract, or the date of the invoice in the absence of any agreement or contract (credit terms should not be taken into consideration).

• When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident

• The date of actual payment

For director’s fees

• When the payment is due and payable under the following scenarios:

◦ Director's fees approved in arrears

For director's fees approved in arrears, the director has already rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned. However, the director's fees must be disclosed to and approved by members of the company before they can be paid to him. Hence, the earliest date on which the director is entitled to the director's fees, is the date the fees are voted and approved at the company's AGM.

◦ Director's fees approved in advance

For director's fees approved in advance, the director may not have rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned when the fees are approved at the company's AGM. Hence, the earliest date on which the director can be entitled to the director's fees, is as and when he renders his services.

•

• When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident

• The date of actual payment

Scenarios | Date of payment to the non-resident  

Filing and payment due date

Technical assistance fees
A non-resident company issued an invoice dated 26 Mar 2025 to a payer for technical assistance fees in respect of services rendered. The invoice stated that the amount must be paid within 30 days.
The payer received the invoice on 30 Apr 2025 and paid the non-resident on 19 May 2025.  | 26 Mar 2025
(based on invoice date)  | 15 May 2025

For GIRO payer, deduction takes place on 26 May 2025.

Royalty payment
The agreement stated that royalties at 5% of sales shall accrue to the non-resident at the end of each quarter.
In this instance, the royalty period from Apr to Jun 2025 was accrued on 30 Jun 2025 (end of quarter), and the royalty payment was made to the non-resident on 15 Jul 2025. | 30 Jun 2025
(based on date of accrual)  | 15 Aug 2025

For GIRO payer, deduction takes place on 25 Aug 2025.

Director’s fee
The director’s fee of $50,000 for the period from 01 Jan 2024 to 31 Dec 2024, was voted and approved in the company's Annual General Meeting (AGM) on 2 Jul 2025.
However, the fee was only paid to the director on 29 Sep 2025.  | 2 Jul 2025
(based on AGM date)  | 15 Sep 2025

For GIRO payer, deduction takes place on 25 Sep 2025.

Multiple payments for a single engagement (non-resident professional or public entertainer)

If you have made multiple payments to the same non-resident professional or non-resident public entertainer for the same engagement within a 60-day period, you can consolidate the various payments into 1 filing and declare the last payment date as the date of payment to the non-resident professional or public entertainer.

Late payment penalty

Penalties will be imposed if the WHT is paid to IRAS after the payment due date or if the GIRO deduction is unsuccessful.

FAQs

Can I consolidate and file my WHT submission?

Yes, you can consolidate and file WHT twice a year, on 15 June and 15 December of each year if you are claiming tax exemption (i.e. tax rate is 0%) under the DTA and ARI.

For example:

Your WHT exempted (i.e. tax rate is 0%) payment to a non-resident is due every 15 of the month. Instead of filing for WHT monthly, you can consolidate and file 6 records on 15 June and the remaining 6 records on 15 December.

outcomes.question: What are the employer and employee CPF percentages in 2026 for a Singapore citizen aged over 60 to 65 earning more than S$750 per month?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Evidence verified

**CPF contribution rates by age group** (party in scope: Employer)
- **CPF rule explanation:** CPF Board’s 2026 contribution table applies from 1 January 2026 to Singapore Citizens or third-year-onward SPRs in private-sector or non-pensionable public-service employment. For monthly wages above S$750, the employer/employee rates are: age 55 and below 17%/20%; above 55 to 60, 16%/18%; above 60 to 65, 12.5%/12.5%; above 65 to 70, 9%/7.5%; above 70, 7.5%/5%. For an actual payroll case, identify the year, birth date, citizenship/PR conversion date and any approved PR-rate election before selecting a table. New age-group rates start on the first day of the month after the 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday. Do not apply this 2026 table to another payroll year. [CPF Contribution Rate Table from 1 January 2026](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/content/dam/web/employer/employer-obligations/documents/CPFcontributionratesfrom1Jan2026.pdf)

**Source:** CPF Contribution Rate Table from 1 January 2026 (live external)

Steps to compute CPF contribution:
1) Compute the total CPF contribution (rounded to the nearest dollar), i.e., to be rounded down for an amount less than 50 cents and rounded up for an amount of 50
cents and above.
2) Compute the employee’s share of CPF contribution (rounded down to the nearest dollar).
3) Employer’s share = Total contribution - Employee’s share
4) If there is only OW payable for the month, the maximum contribution on OW is to be rounded to the nearest dollar for the total CPF contributions and rounded down
to the nearest dollar for employee’s share of CPF contributions. If there are OW and AW payable for the same month, compute and sum up the CPF contributions
that are payable for OW and AW and apply the rounding rules accordingly.
5) To compute CPF contributions, use the CPF contribution calculator (cpf.gov.sg/employer > Tools and services > Calculators > CPF contribution calculator).

to contribute to CPF at full employer- full employee rates.

### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Evidence verified

**CPF contribution rates by age group** (party in scope: Employee)
- **CPF rule explanation:** CPF Board’s 2026 contribution table applies from 1 January 2026 to Singapore Citizens or third-year-onward SPRs in private-sector or non-pensionable public-service employment. For monthly wages above S$750, the employer/employee rates are: age 55 and below 17%/20%; above 55 to 60, 16%/18%; above 60 to 65, 12.5%/12.5%; above 65 to 70, 9%/7.5%; above 70, 7.5%/5%. For an actual payroll case, identify the year, birth date, citizenship/PR conversion date and any approved PR-rate election before selecting a table. New age-group rates start on the first day of the month after the 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday. Do not apply this 2026 table to another payroll year. Updates on 21 May 2026
To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?
The following table summarises the current contribution rates for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third year and onwards) with monthly wages above $750, across the different age groups.
Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34
Above 60 to 65 | 12.5 | 12.5 | 25
Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

Determine your employees’ CPF contributions

Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status

Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion

You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)

An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.

Authority: CPF Board, Government of Singapore
Page title: I have successfully applied for a new re-entry permit and retained my Singapore Permanent Resident status. How will this impact my CPF contributions?
Canonical official URL: https://www.cpf.gov.sg/service/article/i-have-successfully-applied-for-a-new-re-entry-permit-and-retained-my-singapore-permanent-resident-status-how-will-this-impact-my-cpf-contributions
Capture date (Singapore): 2026-10-27
Capture method: verbatim visible text excerpt returned by a read-only browser extraction of the official HTML page. This is not a raw HTML response; exact excerpt text is retained below.

As a Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR), you are required to make CPF contributions on wages earned in Singapore.
CPF contributions are not payable for employees who are neither Singapore Citizens nor SPRs.
Your CPF contribution rates as an SPR depend on how long you have held Permanent Resident status.
First-year rate: Applies from the day you obtain your SPR status, [i.e. the date indicated on your Entry Permit (Form 5/5A) issued by the Immigration & Checkpoints Authority (ICA)] until the last day of the month of your first anniversary of SPR.
Second-year rate: Applies from the month following your first anniversary as an SPR until the last day of the month of your second anniversary.
Third-year rate: Applies from the month following your second anniversary as an SPR onwards.
Example
If you have obtained your SPR status on 15 January 2026, the start and end dates for first, second and third year of obtaining SPR status are shown in the table below:
Year of obtaining SPR status | Starts from | Ends on
First year | 15 January 2026 | 31 January 2027
Second year | 1 February 2027 | 31 January 2028
Third year | 1 February 2028 | Not applicable

outcomes.question: Can payroll deduct the rounded total CPF contribution from the employee and then add an employer share on top?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority **Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed. **General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues. **Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case. **Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment. #### CPF Board — CPF contributions **Status:** Evidence verified **CPF total contribution rounding and employee share recovery** (party in scope: Employer) - **CPF rule explanation:** CPF Board selects the contribution table from citizenship or SPR year, age group and wage band. Total wages combine Ordinary Wages (OW) and Additional Wages (AW), which have separate ceilings. For wages above S$50 and up to S$500 in a month, the employee share is nil but the employer share remains due. Round the combined total contribution to the nearest dollar (50 cents rounds up); drop cents from the employee share and set the employer share to total less employee. To determine the actual amount, supply the payroll month, date of birth, status/PR conversion date, rate election, CPF-classified OW/AW, year-to-date contributions and expected annual OW where an AW ceiling applies. [CPF | How much CPF contributions to pay](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/employer/employer-obligations/how-much-cpf-contributions-to-pay) **Source:** CPF | How much CPF contributions to pay (live external) - **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF total contribution rounding and employee share recovery): CPF | How much CPF contributions to pay

Authority: CPF Board, Government of Singapore
Page title: How much CPF contributions to pay
Canonical official URL: https://www.cpf.gov.sg/employer/employer-obligations/how-much-cpf-contributions-to-pay
Capture date (Singapore): 2026-10-27
Capture method: verbatim visible text returned by a read-only browser extraction of the official HTML page. This is not a raw HTML response; exact excerpt text is retained below.

Updates on 21 May 2026
To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?
The following table summarises the current contribution rates for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third year and onwards) with monthly wages above $750, across the different age groups.
Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34
Above 60 to 65 | 12.5 | 12.5 | 25
Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.
